title: The logic behind the international partnership map
summary: Panos Sousounis argues that if science diplomacy is shaping who UK universities partner with, international strategy teams need three separate assessments running simultaneously
full_text:
Every international office in the sector can produce a map of its institution’s partnerships.

Fewer can explain, with real confidence, why the map looks the way it does. Is a university in a country as a partner because there’s a rising middle class there hungry for a UK-branded degree? Because a bilateral government agreement made it easy? Or because geopolitics has quietly narrowed the field of countries where deep collaboration is even possible?

The honest answer is usually: all three, in shifting proportions, and rarely examined together. I think that’s a problem worth naming, because the calculus behind “who we partner with, and how” is increasingly where science diplomacy actually happens. Not in the roundtables and communiqués, but in the day-to-day decisions international offices and research services teams make about which countries get a joint degree, which get a dual PhD, and which get politely declined.

Three logics competing for the same map

The first driver of partnership choice is straightforwardly demographic and economic: the size and trajectory of a country’s middle class.

Transnational education has grown roughly 70 per cent over the past decade, and the UK’s new International Education Strategy leans hard into TNE and education exports as a route to £40 billion a year by 2030.

That growth has followed demand – a growing aspirational middle class in South and Southeast Asia, the Gulf, and parts of Africa wanting UK-branded qualifications delivered locally, affordably, without relocation. This is the market logic, and it’s real. But it’s also the logic most exposed to competitor risk: if South Korea, Australia or a well-funded local provider offers something cheaper or more locally relevant, market-driven partnerships can evaporate fast.

The second driver is government policy – both the UK’s and the partner country’s.

Regulatory breakthroughs secured through government-to-government engagement, of the kind that opened doors in India, Nigeria, and Saudi Arabia, can turn a country from a difficult market into a strategic priority almost overnight. The reverse is equally true: a partner government tightening its own regulatory environment, or restricting foreign qualification recognition, can freeze years of relationship-building. Universities don’t control this variable at all, which is exactly why so many international strategies read as more coherent in a strategy document than they turn out to be in practice.

The third, and increasingly dominant, driver is geopolitics – and this is where science diplomacy earns its name rather than being a decorative phrase for “international relations, but nicer.” Which countries a UK university can meaningfully partner with on research, and in what fields, is now shaped as much by national security frameworks as by academic merit or market opportunity.

Where the map narrows

This is the part of the conversation the sector is still getting comfortable talking about in public, even though every research office is deep in it privately.

UK export control law, together with the National Security and Investment Act 2021 and the growing research security infrastructure means that a meaningful share of STEM collaboration – anything touching dual-use technology, advanced materials, AI with military application, certain engineering and life sciences fields – now comes with a due diligence and licensing layer that simply didn’t exist a decade ago.

Basic, pre-publication research and taught postgraduate collaboration in sensitive subject areas can require an export licence before a UK academic can even discuss the work in detail with an overseas partner.

None of this is unreasonable in isolation – protecting genuinely sensitive research and guarding against hostile exploitation of open science is a legitimate state interest, and the sector broadly accepts that. But the cumulative effect is that “who we can partner with, and on what” is no longer decided purely by academic judgement. It is co-decided by classification lists, ownership-structure screening, and government risk appetite – and that list of restricted or higher-friction partners tends to track geopolitical rivalry rather than research quality.

The dual role of the humanities

This is where I think the humanities’ place in science diplomacy needs a second, more practical argument, beyond the cultural-bridge-building case I could make elsewhere.

The humanities and social sciences are, for the most part, simply not subject to the same export control and research security architecture as STEM. History, languages, law, economics, cultural studies, philosophy – these disciplines can usually continue to collaborate, teach jointly, and exchange researchers with partner countries in situations where a dual-use engineering or AI partnership would trigger months of licensing review, or wouldn’t clear at all.

That gives the humanities a genuinely dual function in the current environment. The first, familiar function is building the cultural fluency and trust that make any collaboration durable – the argument that science diplomacy is about relationships, not just technical exchange. The second, less discussed function is more structural: when geopolitics closes STEM collaboration with a given country, humanities and social science partnerships can be one of the few channels that stays open. They keep the institutional relationship alive, keep researchers talking to each other, keep the door from closing entirely – so that if and when the geopolitical weather changes, there’s still a functioning relationship to build back on, rather than a cold start.

I’d go further: this makes humanities partnerships not a consolation prize when STEM collaboration is restricted, but a deliberate strategic asset that international offices should be planning for explicitly, rather than treating humanities TNE and research links as the soft add-on to a “real” STEM-led partnership strategy.

How do UK institutions actually decide

If science diplomacy is genuinely shaping who UK universities partner with, the practical implication is that international strategy teams need three separate assessments running simultaneously for any prospective partnership, not one blended judgement. They need a market assessment (is there sustainable demand, and from whom), a policy assessment (what do both governments’ current regulatory postures allow, and how stable is that), and a security assessment (what, if any, of the intended collaboration touches controlled or sensitive territory, and does that change the type of partnership on offer, from joint degree to research consortium to staff exchange).

Where the security assessment narrows what’s possible on the STEM side, the honest move is not to quietly deprioritise the country, but to ask what a humanities or social-science-led partnership could sustain in its place. And that means accepting that its value may be more diplomatic and relational than immediately commercial and building that into how the partnership is resourced and judged.

Universities are not just participants in science diplomacy anymore, whether they intended to be or not – every partnership decision now has a diplomatic dimension attached to it, whether the institution has thought about it in those terms or not.

The sector would do well to make that calculus explicit, rather than leaving it to the separate, rarely connected judgements of admissions, research services, and export control compliance teams.

full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Kathy Collins, Higher Education Consulting Director at Huron, a HEPI Partner.

Transnational education (TNE) – including international branch campuses, joint universities and deeply integrated global partnerships – has become a durable feature of global higher education. Institutions may consider TNE to advance academic mission, expand global reach, support workforce development, diversify revenue and respond to demographic and geopolitical change.

Research by the CrossBorder Education Research Team (C-BERT) confirms the growth and prevalence of these efforts, with hundreds of international branch campuses operating across diverse regulatory, economic, and political environments.

Yet the continued growth of TNE should not be mistaken for uniform success. Outcomes vary significantly, and the distance between an attractive concept and a sustainable operation can be substantial. The central question is therefore not simply where an institution can expand. It is whether the proposed combination of mission, market demand, academic model, governance, economics, and risk can support long-term success.

A feasibility study should test the assumptions, constraints, and tradeoffs that will determine whether an institution should proceed, how the initiative should be designed, and what conditions must be true for it to remain academically credible, financially sustainable, and governable over time.

Seven tests consistently distinguish global TNE strategy feasibility studies that inform sound decisions from those that merely reinforce existing ambitions.

The purpose test

Is the institutional rationale clear enough to guide difficult choices?

Successful TNE initiatives begin with clarity about why the institution is pursuing the opportunity. Efforts framed narrowly around growth or brand visibility struggle to sustain alignment once complexity emerges.

Well-designed feasibility studies define success explicitly before testing market demand or operating models. This discipline ensures that TNE advances institutional strategy rather than substitutes for it.

The governance test

Can the parties agree on control before launch?

Governance is often among the most underestimated determinant of TNE outcomes. Research by C-Bert scholars Kevin Kinser and Jason Lane highlights the importance of oversight arrangements in areas such as faculty, curriculum, and finance, demonstrating that institutions must make deliberate choices about how authority and accountability are shared across borders.

Leading institutions address this risk during feasibility, not after launch. By clearly defining decision rights around academics, escalation, finance, operations and staffing before commitments are made, universities can identify governance constraints early, reduce downstream renegotiation, and create a stronger foundation for long-term success. Feasibility studies that make sure to surface governance constraints early reduce downstream renegotiation and institutional friction.

The academic portability test

Can the model be delivered credibly in the host environment?

Academic models are often the make-or-break variable in TNE, because they carry the institution’s culture, quality norms and labour model – and those do not port automatically across borders.

Three lessons matter most when designing academic models for TNE:

portability is not the same as replicability;

academic model choices drive both quality and economics; and

programme portfolio fit matters more than showcasing institutional prestige.

The sustainable scale test

Can the financial model work beyond the first cohort?

Financial challenges with TNE often stem from unrealistic and misaligned assumptions about enrolment, pricing, cost sharing, external support, or long-term subsidies.

Well-executed feasibility work emphasises conservative assumptions, transparent cost structures, and explicit downside scenarios. Demand modelling must test sustained scale, not just initial interest. A campus must enrol and retain enough students to support a full academic ecosystem.

The decision threshold test

Does the institution know when to proceed, redesign, pause, or stop?

Strong feasibility studies do not simply catalogue risks; they define decisionthresholds. Political, regulatory, reputational and operational risks are assessed alongside conditions under which an institution should pause, redesign or not proceed.

This approach reflects a shift in how institutions now view feasibility: not as justification, but as protection of long-term institutional interests.

The academic legitimacy test

Have academic stakeholders meaningfully tested the model?

TNE initiatives touch the academic core, making academic staff engagement essential. Feasibility studies that meaningfully engage academic stakeholders on curriculum, quality assurance and staffing are better positioned to surface issues early, before institutional commitments are made (Kevin Kinser & Jason Lane, 2014. Managing the oversight of international branch campuses in higher education,” Higher Education Management and Policy, OECD Publishing, vol. 24(3), pages 161-176.)

The lifecycle test

Can the institution adapt, reinvest, resize or exit responsibly?

TNE initiatives rarely unfold exactly as planned. Even well-designed efforts can face predictable inflection points, including launch challenges, financial recalibration, leadership transitions, shifts in partner priorities, and changes in the policy or regulatory environment.

Feasibility should assess whether the institution has the leadership capacity, governance structures, financial resilience, and risk tolerance to navigate the full lifecycle.

What should a feasibility study deliver?

Taken together, these tests show how feasibility work can support TNE decision-making by clarifying the evidence, assumptions, risks and decision thresholds that should inform whether and how an institution proceeds. At its best, a feasibility study should produce:

Objectivity and clarity in go / no-go decisions

Integrated analysis across strategy, academics, finance, and risk

Documented assumptions and evidence gaps

Decision-ready outputs for executive and board governance

The strongest feasibility studies do not simply ask, ‘Can we build a global campus, joint university, or TNE partnership?’ They ask, ‘Should we proceed? Under what conditions? What would need to be true for the initiative to succeed – and what would tell us it is time to reconsider?’

Like late-night study sessions and cramming into a student kitchen to cook up meals, being savvy with money has long been part of the university experience. But with the cost of living remaining high, students are more money-conscious than ever.

“It is one of the most difficult times to make ends meet as a student,” according to Tom Allingham, communications director at Save the Student (STS). He says soaring prices for essentials, such as food and energy bills, have “disproportionately affected” students, while maintenance loans (intended to help cover day-to-day costs) have failed to keep up with high rates of inflation.

STS’s 2025 money survey found the average student spends £1,142 a month on living costs, but receives a maintenance loan of £640, meaning the £502 shortfall has more than doubled since 2020.

So what are the best ways to stretch your loan as far as it will go?

Split money across multiple bank accounts

Opening a student bank account comes with plenty of perks, from free railcards and large interest-free overdrafts to a welcome cash incentive that may come in handy during freshers’ week festivities.

But to stay on top of your spending, don’t keep all of your money in one place. Robert Medhurst, 25, who graduated this summer from Nottingham Trent University, recommends opening a separate digital bank account alongside your main student account, to split your maintenance loan into daily budgets.

Budgeting features on apps such as Monzo, helped him to visualise his finances and rein in his spending, which he found much harder to track when all of his maintenance loan was lumped into one account.

Setting aside money and placing a spending cap on the pots feature – one for rent and others for weekly food shops and nights out – “really allows you to see how much you’re spending and not go over”, he says. It can also help curb the urge for contactless spending.

Make a budget before move-in day

It’s common for students to find themselves tipping into their overdraft faster than expected. To avoid the burden of being in the red, start setting out your budget before you step foot on campus. Allingham suggests incoming students use time over the summer to work out “where the gaps will be in your budget – where potentially you might need to cut back, or where you might need to look for extra income”.

There are plenty of free tools available to help, such as online budget trackers. Soham Chougale, education officer at University College Birmingham Guild of Students, created Your Friendly Guild Budget Buddy to help students keep their finances afloat amid the cost of living crisis. It includes features that help map out income and set saving goals, while offering information on where to access financial and mental health support in one place. “It realistically shows how a student would spend, rather than fancy budget planners which would have 10 other things that are not the top priorities,” says Chougale.

Research hardship funds and bursaries

If you’re experiencing financial difficulty while studying, applying for non-repayable hardship funds and bursaries offered by your university may help ease the strain. In recent years, some universities have doubled or tripled the amount of money in hardship support to students, while also widening the household income criteria for eligibility. Increasingly, says Allingham, institutions have “recognised that it’s not just people from the very poorest backgrounds that are struggling right now”.

For Medhurst, accessing a hardship fund “was a lifesaver”, helping to tide over part of his rent each term. “Don’t be afraid to ask and to look for it,” he says. “There’ll probably be something that you can apply for that can really save you a lot of money.”

Ask for a student discount

Whether stashed away in your wallet or slipped inside your phone case, be sure to keep your student ID on you. Discounts are a big bonus of student life so even if one isn’t advertised, don’t be afraid to wave your ID and ask.

Sign up to student discount platforms like UNiDAYS and Student Beans to enjoy exclusive 10% to 30% offers both in-store and online. Richard Jackson, head of content at Student Beans, says lots of chains such as YO! Sushi, Greene King and Pizza Express offer students in-store dining deals.

The key to securing great discounts, he adds, is to always plan ahead. Follow and set notifications for your favourite brands on discount sites, and keep an eye out for boosted seasonal deals around Freshers, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Start planning your meals

After a long day of lectures, it can be convenient to order a quick meal from Deliveroo or Uber Eats. But relying on takeaway services can add up quickly, totalling an entire week’s food shop in just a single purchase. Instead, 21-year-old Chloe Harmer, a third-year fashion marketing student at Leeds Arts University, found cooking compact meals in bulk to carry around between classes a cost-effective alternative. “I pop it in the fridge and then when I’m about to leave for uni the next day, put it straight in my bag and then that’s lunch sorted,” she says. “And I’d just repeat that most days.”

Before heading off to the supermarket, know exactly what you want. Medhurst researched affordable, simple recipes online and then planned his shopping list around that. “Otherwise you go to Lidl and Aldi just kind of choosing willy-nilly, basing it on what you feel like there and then and it can be very easy to overspend,” he says.

Splurge on discount nights out

You can have a good time without burning through all your student loan. Holly Nicholson, 21, who just graduated with an English literature degree from the University of Bristol, says the key to big nights out on a budget is putting aside in advance how much money to spend on drinks or entry to clubs. And, of course, she says there’s always the old student kitchen tradition: pre-drinking with your flatmates.

Don’t overlook student society socials, which often boast subsidised drinks or free (and fun) events such as film screenings. If you’re a film or theatre devotee like 24-year-old Finola Clarke, an MA journalism student at Goldsmiths, signing up to student memberships at independent cinemas, weekly lottery queues for discounted theatre tickets and scavenging sites like TodayTix and the Stagedoor Rewards app offer some “ways to do what you enjoy at a significantly lower price”, she says.

“You’re in a really weird and hard-adjusting time of your life, don’t put too much pressure on yourself,” says Harmer. “Still have fun, but just be aware of what you’re spending.”

full_text:
Parents and carers in Great Britain spent 12.5% less on school uniform in the run-up to the start of this academic year, turning to promotions and secondhand items to keep expenses down as families struggled with the cost of living crisis.

The average spend on school uniform was £54.53 in the four weeks to 6 September, down an eighth from £62.29 in the same period last year, according to the market research company Worldpanel by Numerator. Overall grocery inflation picked up to 2.3% from 2.1%.

Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at the company, said “value is the watchword for parents this back-to-school season” as they try to balance stretched household budgets.

Almost half of households (44%) prioritised keeping costs low above all else when it comes to buying uniform, even if that means compromising on quality, while a third (33%) aimed to strike a balance between the two, according to a back-to-school survey conducted by Worldpanel in August.

“It’s a clear sign that, for many families, the return to school is landing at a difficult time financially, and retailers who can offer reassurance on price without compromising on quality stand will stand in good stead,” McKevitt said.

Grocery sales rose 2% year on year over the period, the monthly Worldpanel figures showed. August brought more warm weather and the end of a summer of sport. But with the return to school and work looming for many, shopping habits began to shift. Shoppers made 18m fewer trips to supermarkets compared with a peak of 497m in July.

“The end of the summer holidays typically brings a cooling in trip frequency and a pivot towards priority purchases, and this year is no exception,” McKevitt said. “While grocery inflation ticked up modestly last month, it remains significantly lower than the levels we saw earlier in the year, giving households some welcome breathing room.”

Sandwiches featured in more than half of all kids’ lunchboxes, with more than half a million more households that include children buying loaves of bread in the seven days to 6 September compared with the previous week. The number buying satsumas (+29%) and cucumbers (+21%) also rose in the final week before the return to school.

Sales at Asda rose by 0.1% over the 12 weeks to 6 September, as the grocer returned to growth for the first time since March 2024. However, the Leeds-based retailer’s market share dipped to 11.5%.

The online supermarket Ocado, with sales up by 13.3%, remained the fastest-growing grocer overall, with a slightly higher market share of 2.2%. Lidl moved up to 8.7% of the market.

Sainsbury’s and Morrisons maintained their previous market share of 15.2% and 8.4%, respectively. The UK’s largest supermarket, Tesco, dipped to 27.8% from 28.1%. The German discounter Aldi took a 10.6% share.

title: OPINION: I’m a college president, and I think higher education has to do a better job of controlling costs

The post OPINION: I’m a college president, and I think higher education has to do a better job of controlling costs appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Every fall, millions of American parents and caregivers make extraordinary sacrifices to send a child to college. They work overtime, postpone retirement, take on debt or set aside other priorities because they believe higher education can create opportunities they never had.

Students make sacrifices too. Many work nights and weekends, juggle family responsibilities or borrow against their future because they believe a college degree is worth it.

Those sacrifices deserve accountability. And it’s time for colleges to provide it.

For too long, colleges and universities have responded to growing public skepticism by defending the value of higher education. We produce reports, commentaries and a lot of billboards explaining why college still matters; we remind families that graduates earn more than nongraduates over their lifetimes and celebrate the role universities play in preparing the workforce.

Every one of those arguments is true. They simply miss the point.

Most Americans recognize a degree has value. What they increasingly question is whether today’s universities have earned the right to charge what they do. They feel defeated by colleges that raise tuition more readily than they reduce bureaucracy. They chafe at institutions that scrutinize family finances more rigorously than their own budgets.

Too often, university leaders assume declining public confidence can be reversed solely through better messaging. It cannot. Trust is earned through disciplined stewardship and measurable results.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Families are right to expect universities to treat every tuition dollar with the same care they bring to their personal finances.

Students are right to expect that their degree will open the door to opportunity and that earning it won’t burden them with a debt they carry into adulthood.

Taxpayers are right to expect institutions to operate efficiently and demonstrate measurable value.

Universities are good at explaining why costs are unavoidable, but they are reluctant to ask whether every cost is justified. Before asking families to pay more, every university president and chancellor should first answer one question.

What have we done to deserve that investment?

Related: If higher education wants to rebuild public trust, start with making college affordable

The value of affordability is a lesson I’ve learned throughout my career in higher education leadership, first as executive vice president for research and partnerships at Purdue University, then as president of the University of Vermont and now at the University of Arizona. In my time serving at these institutions over the past 14 years, there have been no across-the-board tuition increases.

Purdue froze tuition in 2013 and that freeze remains in place today. While at Vermont, we froze all tuition and fees for all students for five years. At Arizona, we have held resident undergraduate tuition flat for three consecutive years while eliminating a $177 million budget deficit and restoring the university’s financial foundation.

Those outcomes didn’t happen because higher education suddenly became less expensive. They happened because we made intentionally different choices.

To eliminate the deficit and restore financial sustainability at Arizona, we cut administrative spending by more than 20 percent; dissolved inefficient, multimillion-dollar administrative units; and challenged ourselves to operate leaner, including a comprehensive evaluation of all leadership positions that reduced the number of vice president positions to three.

At the same time, we strengthened transfer pathways with community colleges, introduced accelerated three-year medical and veterinary degree programs to address critical workforce shortages and expanded flexible online programs to reduce both the cost and the time required to earn a University of Arizona degree.

Every unnecessary dollar a university spends is a dollar that a family must earn, save or borrow. Those choices carry a human cost. They mean more debt, more financial pressure and greater sacrifice for the families who place their trust in us. Universities should spend tuition dollars with the same discipline families use when deciding whether they can afford college in the first place.

A university education must deliver far more than a diploma. It must prepare graduates for meaningful careers while equipping them with the judgment, resilience, adaptability and perspective to thrive in a rapidly changing world.

That is why Arizona is leveraging philanthropic contributions and strengthening industry partnerships to expand internships and experiential learning and significantly increase study abroad opportunities for students whose financial circumstances would otherwise keep those experiences beyond their reach.

Opportunity should not depend on a family’s income. It should be part of what every great public university provides.

Elite private universities dominate the national conversation about higher education while educating only a tiny fraction of America’s students. They are extraordinary institutions that deserve credit for their achievements. But they are not the institutions that will determine whether most Americans can afford or obtain a college degree.

Related: America’s regional universities can still be a bargain in a sea of high-priced options

That responsibility and privilege belong to flagship public universities. We educate millions of students from every background and create opportunities at a scale no other sector can match. Our defining strength is not exclusivity. It is excellence at scale delivered at a price families can afford.

The American people are asking universities for something reasonable. Challenge costs before raising prices. Reduce bureaucracy before financing it. Measure success by the opportunities we create, not simply the number of students we enroll.

When public universities make those choices, states should respond by investing more in the students they educate. That investment is not a subsidy for the institutions. It is a down payment on the workforce, economic competitiveness and civic leadership every state needs.

Public funding should reward institutions that produce results and the lion’s share of America’s degrees while responsibly managing taxpayer and tuition dollars.

Americans shouldn’t have to trust higher education because university presidents tell them to. They should trust us because our actions leave them no other conclusion.

Suresh Garimella serves as the 23rd president of the University of Arizona and University Distinguished Professor in the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

title: Auburn Faculty Protest Board’s Curricular Overhaul
summary:
Auburn Faculty Protest Board’s Curricular Overhaul
Emma Whitford Tue, 09/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

Three months after the Board of Trustees abolished the faculty senate and gave itself curricular control, faculty are back on campus and making their disapproval known.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
With the fall semester now in full swing, Auburn University faculty members are protesting the Board of Trustees’ summer overhaul of shared governance and curricular decision-making at the public land-grant university in Alabama. More than 160 faculty and community members gathered outside the board’s quarterly meeting on Friday to make their objections visible to trustees and administrators, who faculty say have downplayed their disapproval of the new policies.

In early June, Auburn’s board abruptly dissolved the faculty senate and gave itself complete control over course offerings, curriculum, degree requirements and academic credentials, mirroring the actions of public university boards in other conservative states. At the time, some accused Auburn of preemptively overcomplying with a state law—House Bill 580—that doesn’t apply to the university.

“We really care about Auburn University, and I care about my students, and from what I’m seeing from the actions of the board—especially since June 5th—I’m worried about the future of the institution,” said Tracy Witte, a psychological sciences professor and member of United Campus Workers, the union that coordinated Friday’s protest.

Most faculty members—many of whom work on nine-month contracts that end in May—were not on campus when the board approved the sweeping changes, Witte said. UCW and the Auburn University Chapter of the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) have “made a lot of efforts over the summer to just catch people up on what exactly happened and what the ramifications are.”

Lisa Kensler, an educational leadership professor and former chair of the faculty senate, said she was “crushed” when she learned the senate had been dissolved.

Though not all faculty may realize it immediately, “it’s a pretty important organizational structure that we’ve lost,” Kensler said. “The staff maintain their shared governance structure. The administrative and professional employees maintain theirs. The students maintain theirs. It’s only the faculty that lost their structure for collective voice and contribution.”

Despite widespread disapproval of the changes, faculty members have been frightened to speak publicly against the policies, several professors told Inside Higher Ed. Witte described a “culture of fear” that’s infected Auburn over the past year. Kate Craig, an associate professor of history, said that faculty were scared into silence last fall, when Auburn fired several employees over their social media posts about the late conservative firebrand Charlie Kirk.

“That was a moment where all employees at Auburn realized that Auburn was willing to fire them within a week of making private statements and doing private actions on social media,” Craig said. “Since that moment, we’ve all been very aware of what the president is willing to do.”

Without an outspoken faculty body, administrators have assumed that professors largely support—or are at least indifferent to—the changes, Witte said.

“What we’re hearing from [administrators] is, ‘Oh, it’s only a few people that are concerned about this’ … but based on the conversations I’ve been having around campus, that is not the case,” she said. “Almost everyone I talk to is very concerned, but they [think] they can’t say anything.”

Last week, UCW and AAUP leaders wrote a joint statement that they intended to read during Friday’s board meeting, but their request to speak was denied without explanation, said Heidi Hausse, an associate professor of history at Auburn. Instead, they delivered the statement to administrators on Friday morning.

“Over the past several months, the Board has made significant changes without faculty participation,” it read. “These actions represent a shift away from shared responsibility and toward increasingly centralized control. As faculty, we have found ourselves asking, ‘Is this Auburn?’”

“Is this Auburn?” was a common refrain during Friday’s visibility event, where faculty and supporters lined up along the sidewalk and held signs that read “Excellence taking a backseat to control,” “Educational decisions without educators,” and Putting politics in our classrooms,” all followed by a rhetorical, “Is this Auburn?”

UCW has also been circulating a “declaration of concern,” similar to the union’s statement, which union leaders sent to the provost and Board of Trustees after the event Friday. As of Monday afternoon, the declaration had garnered nearly 700 signatures.

UCW and AAUP haven’t received a response from administrators or trustees, said Hausse. All the faculty members who spoke to Inside Higher Ed said they were pessimistic that they would hear anything in response to the statement or declaration.

Auburn spokespeople did not return a request for comment Monday.

“I don’t think it’s Pollyanna of me to imagine that the president could have come by, shook hands, and said, ‘Hi, I appreciate what you’re here for, I appreciate that you’re working in service to Auburn,’” Kensler said. “I think he really missed an important leadership opportunity to help cultivate a bridge, but maybe that will happen in the future in some way.”

Jessica Blake
full_text:
Starting next fall, thousands of students at Carleton College, a selective private institution in Minnesota, will no longer be expected to take out federal or institutional loans to finance their education.

Instead, the college plans to cover 100 percent of the remaining cost after a family pays its expected family contribution using other forms of aid like grants, scholarships, and student employment, according to a Monday announcement. The policy change will apply to new students as well as current freshman, sophomores and juniors who return. About 2,128 undergraduates attended Carleton in fall 2024, according to federal data.

“As a liberal arts college that prepares students for a wide variety of futures, we want students to know that whatever path they choose to follow, they will begin without any burden of debt to limit their options,” Carleton president Alison Byerly said in a news release. “We believe that a family’s finances should never determine a student’s ability to attend Carleton, and we’re proud to be one of a small number of colleges nationwide with the resources to make this possible.”

Carleton is the first Minnesota college to make this commitment and one of about 20 institutions nationwide, many of which are members of the Ivy League, according to the release.

The transition to a no-loan model was made possible by donations from alumni and other supporters who committed over $80 million over the past 10 months. Now the college is seeking an additional $48 million to sustain the policy and continue supporting low- and middle-income families long-term.

More than half of Carleton students receive need-based aid to cover the full cost of attendance. According to the news release, the average aid awarded for this academic year was $71,870, though it’s unclear how much of that was loan-based. The total cost of attendance was around $97,870, according to the college’s website.

“We recognize the increasing cost of a college education for students and their families, and we see this as a moment for Carleton to fulfill its ongoing desire to be more accessible and affordable for all students who are receiving aid—not just those with the greatest need,” said Art Rodriguez, a Carleton alum and now dean of admissions and financial aid.

title: 4 Ways to Rethink When Student Support Starts
summary:
4 Ways to Rethink When Student Support Starts
Joshua.Bay Tue, 09/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

New initiatives and research show how colleges can reach students earlier and extend support across more of their higher ed journey.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges have traditionally concentrated different kinds of support around predictable moments: the transition into college, the first year, when students ask for help or as they near graduation. But recent initiatives and research suggest that starting those interventions earlier or extending them across more of the student journey can improve outcomes.

Whether by awarding college credit for career-readiness learning completed in high school or extending first-generation support into sophomore year, colleges are experimenting with ways to reach students sooner and build support across different stages of their education.

Here are four ways colleges are rethinking when to start student support.

Start tracking college progress before enrollment.

Giving students college credit for career-readiness learning they’re already doing can achieve more than give them a head start on a degree. For students who may not see college as an option, Maine’s public universities are betting that having credits in hand could change their whole perspective on whether a degree is within reach.

Starting this fall, the University of Maine System will award academic credit for microcredentials earned by high school students through Jobs for Maine’s Graduates (JMG), a statewide nonprofit that helps students transition into college or meaningful careers.

Through the agreement, students can earn up to eight college credits for JMG microcredentials that demonstrate mastery of such skills as financial and digital literacy, entrepreneurship and leadership development.

The initiative is aimed especially at students who may not already see college as part of their future. JMG serves more than 13,000 students annually, and most enter the program without plans to attend college, according to the organization.

Kimberley Acker Lipp, President and CEO of JMG, said nearly 70 percent of the students the organization serves come from economically disadvantaged households where neither parent attended college.

“They don’t see themselves as college-going, and then underneath that, they don’t understand the different pathways that are available to them to get to college,” Lipp said. “This [JPG] engenders confidence, and it also creates a new understanding and fluency of the postsecondary pathways that are available to them.”

Extend support beyond the first year.

First-generation students can face a range of challenges in college, from financial barriers and feelings of isolation to navigating complex university systems without the guidance of family members who have done so before. Colleges often address those barriers through dedicated programs that provide first-year students with cohort-based courses, mentoring and other supports.

But that support can drop off after the first year, even as students begin making consequential decisions about their majors and careers. The University of Michigan believes that adding support during sophomore year can improve outcomes for first-gen students.

The university’s College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) is launching LSA First Fellows, a cohort-based program designed to connect first-generation sophomores with resources, mentors and opportunities on campus. The program will officially begin in January and is open to all domestic first-generation sophomores in the college.

First Fellows will provide students with a one-credit course, team-based mentoring and community events, as well as $4,000 to pursue an experiential learning opportunity during the summer after their sophomore year. Supported by philanthropy, the funding will be available to every participant regardless of financial need.

LSA Dean Rosario Ceballo said the idea for First Fellows grew out of conversations with first-generation students who described a gap in support after their first year.

“When you get to college in the first year, you’re often in a residence hall, you’ve got peer mentors and advisers, all of the university clubs want you to join, everybody comes to your classes and everybody is excited,” Ceballo said.

“But when I was doing focus groups and talking to a lot of first-gen students, one of the things that they said to me at the time was ‘There’s all this support and attention in the first year,’” she added. “‘Then in sophomore year, you’re like, where did it all go?’”

Spot problems before students reach a crisis.

Students often leave clues that they’re struggling before they stop attending classes or exit college altogether. But those warning signs can be scattered across different offices and data systems, making it difficult for college staff to see the full picture or intervene before a student reaches a crisis point.

Some colleges are exploring whether artificial intelligence can help connect those dots and make student support more proactive. Austin Community College, for one, is testing a new initiative designed to identify student needs earlier.

The public two-year institution recently announced the Digital Twin Initiative, a partnership with the Trellis Foundation, a Texas-based nonprofit, aimed at using AI and real-time student data to identify potential barriers before they derail a student’s progress. An $875,000 grant from the foundation will support the initiative.

The college plans to integrate information from across its systems to create a more holistic picture of individual students’ experiences, helping staff identify emerging needs and connect students more quickly with advising, tutoring, financial aid, mental health services and basic-needs resources. This fall, ACC is rolling out an initial version of the platform to roughly 46,000 active credit students, with additional features planned for the spring.

Russell Lowery-Hart, chancellor of Austin Community College, said the goal isn’t to replace direct interactions between students and college staff, but to shift away from a model that largely depends on students to initiate those conversations.

“Nothing is going to replace a direct conversation with a student,” Lowery-Hart said. “But right now, almost all of those conversations rely on the student reaching out, scheduling and identifying, and that’s the shift we’re trying to make.”

Begin career preparation before senior year.

Students who understand how their skills, interests and education connect to a range of career pathways may be better positioned to navigate a rapidly changing job market, according to recent research from the DeBruce Foundation.

The report from the nonprofit, which focuses on expanding pathways to economic growth and opportunity, found that people with higher degrees of career literacy—the ability to understand, plan and navigate career pathways—conduct broader job searches, are more open to changing careers over time and experience greater employment security. Those skills, researchers argue, will become increasingly important as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the labor market.

According to the findings, individuals with high career literacy considered about six potential jobs during a job search, compared to roughly two among those with low career literacy. The research also found that people with both strong career literacy and robust professional networks explored 22 percent more career options outside their current path than their peers and earned an average of $40,000 more annually.

Leigh Anne Taylor Knight, executive director and CEO of the DeBruce Foundation, said introducing students to career literacy early in their college experience can help them understand the range of career opportunities available to them and connect their coursework to future careers.

“Exposing them to new industries and different kinds of professions, as well as helping them see the relevance of what they’re doing in their coursework, just turns them on to be able to attain those degrees,” she said. “When you see that there’s a wide opportunity of ways that [you] can use this degree, you’re more likely to be excited about completing that degree.”

title: Featured Gig: Learning Design at Brown University
summary:
Featured Gig: Learning Design at Brown University joshua.m.kim@d… Tue, 09/15/2026 - 03:00 AM

4 questions for Melissa Kane, Director of Online Program Development.

Byline(s)
Joshua Kim
full_text:
If you are searching for a learning designer, I will always be interested in highlighting the role in this Featured Gig series. Please get in touch. When my friend and long-time colleague, Melissa Kane, Director of Online Program Development at Brown, shared that she is searching for a learning designer, it was a total no-brainer to feature the role here.

Q1: What is the university’s mandate behind this role? How does it help align with and advance the university’s strategic priorities?

A1: Brown’s online graduate degree programs advance the university’s teaching mission by reaching learners who cannot pursue a residential degree in Providence, R.I. The learning designer joins the Digital Learning & Design (DLD) Online team, which partners with academic leadership and Brown faculty across many academic departments on high-touch, end-to-end course design and faculty development.

The unit was established five years ago and now supports six programs with more on the way. As the portfolio has matured, DLD Online’s work has expanded beyond simply launching programs to now building, sustaining and refining them, and this position contributes to that next phase of redefining our service models and developing new approaches to online instruction.

The learning designer role sits within Brown’s framework of Building on Distinction and aligns with several of the Provost’s articulated priorities. Brown has committed to a distinctive and responsible approach to generative AI in teaching and learning, and the learning designer role reflects that commitment by helping faculty think critically about discipline-specific AI literacy and ways in which to amplify human-centered learning experiences in an online setting.

Q2: Where does the role sit within the university structure? How will the person in this role engage with other units and leaders across campus? Is the role in-person, hybrid or remote-eligible?

A2: The learning designer is a member of DLD Online, a cross-functional team of nearly twenty learning designers, learning technologists, and media producers within the Sheridan Center for Teaching and Learning. Learning designers work in project-based groups alongside media editors, videographers and learning technologists.

The role is engaged across academic departments and disciplines. A learning designer is likely to work concurrently with faculty in the School of Public Health, the Thomas J. Watson Jr. School of International and Public Affairs, and the Data Science Institute, as well as program staff and academic directors. The learning designer also engages with campus partners from the Brown Library, the School of Professional Studies and the Office of Information Technology as course projects require.

This position is hybrid, requiring at least one day on campus per week, with Tuesdays serving as our team-wide in-person day.

Q3: What would success look like in one year? Three years? Beyond?

A3: In one year, the learning designer has completed course development in more than one program, established productive working relationships with faculty, and demonstrated fluency in the team’s tools and standards, including WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility and technical remediation.

Within three years, the learning designer contributes to the unit’s innovation and its response to emerging trends in online teaching and learning, consistent with our core values. They have developed a recognized area of expertise, shaped by their interests and institutional need, for which they are known within the team and across the university.

Beyond year three, the learning designer has contributed significantly to articulating what sustainable, responsible innovation in online learning looks like at Brown, in ways that persist beyond individual courses and contribute to the online graduate programs as a whole.

Q4: What kinds of future roles would someone who took this position be prepared for?

A4: Because the learning designer position combines pedagogical expertise and consultation with hands-on technical development, it develops a set of capacities that are rare in more conventional instructional design roles.

We’ve already had folks advance into director and associate director roles in teaching and learning centers, and, more broadly, the same profile prepares learning designers for roles in faculty development, educational technology, and learning experience design roles in industry and nonprofit organizations.

title: EAIE: National strategies sharpen focus on talent, but autonomy stays non‑negotiable
summary:
European governments are refining their internationalisation strategies with a view to attract and retain talent. But at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow, sector leaders from the UK, Germany and Slovenia underlined that universities still expect – and need – room to set their own course.

The post EAIE: National strategies sharpen focus on talent, but autonomy stays non‑negotiable appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For the UK, the language has shifted away from headline student targets, but not away from internationalisation as a strategic lever.

“Internationalisation needs to be seen as a strategic enabler, and as a soft power asset,” said Rachel Sandison, deputy vice-chancellor (external engagement) at the University of Glasgow.

Sandison works with two overlapping strategies – the UK government’s refreshed international education strategy and the Scottish government’s international education strategy, launched in 2024 and currently being refreshed.

“There is a very high degree of complementarity between both governments in thinking beyond just student recruitment and student mobility when exploring and supporting all things international,” she told the Glasgow audience gathered for the 2026 European Association of International Education (EAIE) conference.

The UK has removed explicit international student number targets, but still has an education export target of £40 billion by 2030. Alongside this, recent migration policy changes are framed under the banner of “sustainable recruitment”.

Scotland, meanwhile, is placing a strong emphasis on talent attraction.

“Within the Scottish context, there is a real drive to bring global talent to these shores… to really signal Scotland as a welcoming, diverse and inclusive country for study, for research, to work, to live,” said Sandison.

There has also been a shift in who is involved nationally. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office is now a formal partner in the UK strategy.

“They are seen as one of the key government partners within the strategy, which wasn’t true before. So it has really shifted.”

Meanwhile, Germany’s 2024-2034 national strategy for the internationalisation of higher education is built around attraction and retention, even in a system where higher education is largely governed at state level.

“Germany has the 16 states, and the states are governing universities in Germany. So the national government doesn’t have to say too much about universities,” explained Kai Sicks, secretary general of the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD).

Despite this federal complexity, federal and state governments, DAAD and other stakeholders agreed a joint strategy.

“The number one priority of this strategy is to increase the attractiveness of Germany as a nation for internationals… retaining students in Germany is a top priority.”

The number one priority of this strategy is to increase the attractiveness of Germany as a nation for internationals… retaining students in Germany is a top priority.

Kai Sicks, DAAD

“It talks a lot about how it would like to create framework conditions, also on a legal regulatory basis, to improve the ability to attract students – like we improve visa accessibility of Germany, to make all these bureaucratic procedures more easy.”

He pointed to a new DAAD program, funded by the responsible ministry, that supports almost 100 universities with activities to help international students complete their studies and stay in Germany. The “ground for that was laid in the strategy”, he said.

Meanwhile, Slovenia has moved from a mobility‑focused strategy to a broader, more integrated approach covering both higher education and research.

The first strategy (2016-2020) was mainly about mobility and visibility, but already introduced internationalisation at home. The current 2023-2030 strategy shifts towards long‑term institutional partnerships and stronger links within Europe, while also expanding geographically.

“The Western Balkans is still the major priority… but we also added Africa and East Asia and Canada and Australia and many other countries. So I think in this regard we are a very ambitious little country,” said Alenka Flander, director, the Centre of the Republic of Slovenia for Mobility and European Educational and Training Programs (CMEPIUS).

“Resources are always sparse, but still we have ambitions to kind of focus on quite big regions.”

In Slovenia, the foreign ministry was not strongly involved in the strategy, which helps explain its focus on education and research rather than broader foreign policy objectives.

Flander cautioned that ambition needs to be balanced with realism at both national and institutional levels and across the discussion, speakers were clear that institutional autonomy remains a core principle.

“Universities really have a very high degree of institutional autonomy… strategy making within a university is an independent process,” said Sicks. “At the same time, a national strategy can serve as orientation or a compass.”

Sandison echoed that national frameworks can be helpful as long as they do not become overly prescriptive. “Institutions should have the flexibility and autonomy to consider how they respond to them, and where they want to really lean in, and where actually some of that national framework may not make sense,” she said.

In the UK, she now sits on an International Education Strategy Action Group which aims to make the framework more concrete.

“It actually then makes that national framework much more tangible and meaningful because it’s not just a lot of nice words on a page, but it’s trying to translate the strategic ambition into something practical in support of the sector.”

title: Cultivating Student Resilience: Practical Strategies for Well-Being
summary:
The introduction of self-regulation and stress-management strategies into higher education curricula has recently come into focus as a necessary component of promoting resilience and preventing future professional burnout (Hsu & Goldsmith, 2021; Egan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025). In addition to enhancing academic performance, evidence-based regulation strategies could help mitigate the effects of […]

The post Cultivating Student Resilience: Practical Strategies for Well-Being appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The introduction of self-regulation and stress-management strategies into higher education curricula has recently come into focus as a necessary component of promoting resilience and preventing future professional burnout (Hsu & Goldsmith, 2021; Egan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025). In addition to enhancing academic performance, evidence-based regulation strategies could help mitigate the effects of the high-stakes, high-stress environment inherent in college and post-graduate education (Chongjin et al., 2025), and learned self-regulation skills may carry over into the professional environment after graduation (Emerson et al., 2023). Integrating short, reflective activities and simple self-regulation practices into established curricula may be an effective strategy for providing students with helpful and actionable means to foster self-awareness and well-being (Egan et al., 2021; Gilani, 2025). This article aims to discuss how stress management can be a tool for building resilience and promoting deep learning, outline several practical approaches that educators can use to weave self-care into existing curricula, and introduce several strategies to foster students’ self-exploration and awareness.

Unmanaged and excessive stress impairs the cognitive flexibility needed for deep learning (Zhang et al., 2025).To mitigate these effects on students, resilience skills such as cognitive reframing and emotional regulation can be taught as effective techniques to support academic success (Egan et al., 2022).

Many of the self-reflection skills that help increase stress tolerance are closely linked to those of metacognition, a fundamental component of self-regulated learning (SRL). In a systematic review of interventions to improve SRL, 74% of the analyzed interventions focused on metacognitive skills as a means of supporting self-regulation in students (Simón-Grábalos et al., 2025). SRL boosts confidence, enhances critical thinking, and improves student performance. SRL also helps learners develop essential career skills such as solving complex problems and effective time management (Gagnon et al, 2026).

Teaching adult learners basic principles of brain function and neuroplasticity may help them reframe stress, regulate emotions, and improve self-efficacy and optimism for change (Tabibnia, 2024). Leveraging the brain’s ability to reorganize in response to practiced experiences can be framed for learners as a viable pathway to build resilience and manage stressors. This strategy reflects the concept of growth mindset-a belief that intelligence is both malleable and improvable (Ng, 2018). Thus, emphasizing and encouraging a growth mindset could be a powerful tool for helping learners navigate both academic and future professional challenges.

Demanding schedules and packed curricula make it difficult for students and educators to prioritize stress management and wellness practices, despite recognizing their inherent value (Chongjin et al., 2025). Transitioning from a theoretical understanding of the importance of self-care to the practical application of building student resilience, requires stress management to be viewed and treated as a professional competence rather than an individual responsibility (Jian et al., 2025). Intentionally integrating self-care concepts and methods into existing course curricula and resources is a key to normalizing the prioritization of mental, emotional, and physical health for students. The following actionable methods for embedding self-care initiatives into existing class time are simple and effective.

Syllabus Resourcing

Include a section on the front page of each course syllabus that acknowledges the demands of the course. Explicitly list campus mental health resources and encourage their use.

Embracing Error

Making mistakes is an important component of learning. Changing the wording when addressing errors is a simple way to create an inclusive learning environment and build critical thinking skills (Chong et al., 2025)

Be curious: “What makes you say that?” Encourages sharing and dialogue, allowing faculty to give feedback that focuses on critical thinking and processing skills, rather than the binary view of “right” and “wrong”.

Normalizing Uncertainty

Ambiguity is a hallmark of many professions, and building tolerance for it is a critical skill. Letting students know that knowing how to find a reliable answer to a question or solution to a problem is often more valuable and important than knowing the answer immediately (Ng, 2018). Incorporating case-based learning with multiple plausible approaches is an effective way to model this principle for students (Hsu & Goldsmith, 2021).

Model Vulnerability

Hearing faculty share their professional missteps or errors and how they were corrected or turned into learning moments is a powerful way to come alongside students and show that mistakes are not personal failings, and to model their effective use.

Physical Grounding Techniques

Lead short, evidence-based physical grounding techniques to help students decrease tension and stress (Bently et al., 2023).

Box breathing (American Heart Association, 2024).

Body scan (Masterclass, 2022).

Somatic self care (Johns Hopkins Medicine, n.d.).

Scan for Signals

Encourage students to take a moment prior to tests and quizzes to “scan” their emotional state and stress level help them become aware of and monitor their emotional and physical responses to stressful situations. Encourage them to use physical grounding techniques before, during, and after high-stakes testing.

Write it Down

Promote short reflective journaling assignments, giving prompts to help students identify what study techniques work for them, what areas of their training cause the most stress (Gilani, 2025; Sage & Sele, 2015), and help by suggesting possible solutions or avenues of exploration, including seeking higher levels of care with professional counseling.

Create Community

Provide short prompts for structured, time-limited peer conversations where students discuss both course topics and the emotional stressors of the week. (Chong et al, 2025; Gómez et al, 2024).

Cultivating resilience in students prepares them for lifelong learning and normalizes the practices of attending to personal wellness and maintaining mental health. By incorporating simple practices into classroom curricula and placing value on self-reflection, the role of making mistakes as part of a natural learning process, and showing students how stress can prevent deep learning, educators can provide life skills that could help prevent burnout in professional practice (Chong et al., 2025).
